title: Week 2 Mastery Quiz — Geography and Human Systems

questions.prompt: Which example gives an absolute location?
choices: south of the river
near the old market
two hours from the coast
questions.explanation: Absolute location uses a fixed reference such as geographic coordinates; the other choices describe relative location.

questions.prompt: A geographer says a town is upstream from a port and east of a mountain pass. Which concept is being used?
choices: Projection
Relative location
Scale
Population density
questions.explanation: Relative location describes a place in relation to other places or features.

questions.prompt: Why does map scale matter when interpreting distance?
choices: It identifies the map's political viewpoint.
It determines which projection is automatically correct.
It shows the relationship between distance on the map and distance on Earth.
It proves why people migrated.
questions.explanation: Scale translates mapped distance into real-world distance. It does not by itself explain politics, projection choice, or migration causes.

questions.prompt: Why must every flat world map distort at least some geographic property?
choices: Cartographers intentionally make maps inaccurate.
Political borders change too quickly.
Latitude and longitude cannot be measured.
Earth's curved surface cannot be flattened without tradeoffs in area, shape, distance, or direction.
questions.explanation: Map projections transform a curved surface into a flat one, so every projection preserves some properties better than others.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes human-environment interaction?
choices: People adapt to, depend on, and alter natural systems, while environments create possibilities and constraints.
Environment determines exactly how every society will develop.
Human choices are independent of geography.
Only climate matters in settlement decisions.
questions.explanation: Human-environment interaction is reciprocal: geography matters, but technology, institutions, culture, and power shape how people respond.

questions.prompt: A population-density map shows a large concentration near a coast. What is the strongest next step before explaining why?
choices: Assume the coast caused the settlement pattern.
Compare additional evidence such as water access, transport routes, terrain, economic activity, and political boundaries.
Ignore the pattern because maps are simplified.
Conclude the population is permanent and never seasonal.
questions.explanation: A mapped pattern is an observation, not yet a complete causal explanation. Multiple geographic and human-system variables should be tested.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows why migration is rarely explained by one factor alone?
choices: A traveler chooses a road because it is shorter.
A map uses a different color scheme.
A family moves because conflict creates risk, relatives provide a destination network, transportation becomes available, and border rules allow entry.
A city lies at an absolute location.
questions.explanation: Migration often reflects interacting push factors, pull factors, networks, transportation, policy, and constraints.

questions.prompt: A conformal projection preserves local shape and direction well but greatly enlarges high-latitude areas. Which conclusion is most responsible?
choices: The map is useless.
The projection is the only accurate world map.
Area comparisons made from the map are automatically exact.
The projection may be useful for some navigation or shape tasks but should not be used uncritically for comparing land area.
questions.explanation: Projection choice should match purpose. A map can be useful for one task while distorting another property.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best help test a claim that a new highway changed migration into a region?
choices: One person's opinion about the highway
Migration counts before and after the highway, transportation data, and evidence about other changes occurring at the same time
A world map with no time data
The highway's name
questions.explanation: Testing change over time requires before/after evidence and attention to competing explanations rather than one anecdote or static map.

questions.prompt: Which statement best answers the week's essential question without geographic determinism?
choices: Location determines human choices completely.
Geography matters only when technology is absent.
Location creates opportunities and constraints, but people respond through technology, institutions, culture, networks, and power.
Places with similar environments always develop in the same way.
questions.explanation: Geography influences choices and risks without mechanically determining outcomes; human systems mediate environmental possibilities and constraints.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least two specific examples from this week, explain how location can shape opportunities, risks, movement, and human choices without determining them completely. Include one limitation of a map, dataset, or geographic explanation.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a clear claim, accurately uses at least two Week 2 concepts or examples such as scale, projection, settlement pattern, migration factors, transportation, or human-environment interaction, explains the relationship rather than merely listing evidence, and identifies one limit or alternative factor.
